The residues first: the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks are named as the slow rotting ones to avoid in the residue layer, and what should go there is the fast kind, chopped, being straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea. The order second: the build is a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of chopped residues trodden down well, then topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator. The watering third: each layer is watered as it is laid, because water poured over a finished heap runs off the outside and leaves the middle dry, which is exactly what you found. The four points are the signs that tell you the disease is Newcastle, and the second to fifth are the signs that tell you the disease is fowl pox or the disease carried by a mosquito.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists them: drowsiness, loss of appetite, dullness, sad demeanor, drooping wings and feathers, keeping away from the flock, not feeding, thin, breathing hard, and diarrhoea. It also says to isolate the sick birds, forbid any trading in your henhouse, inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly, and never eat the carcasses. The 2017 ESFT compendium adds those: a dead bird in the corner, with its head raised, is a sign to show to the veterinary service.

per_item.reference: No, the cycles overlap. A bird takes twenty-one days of incubation and then six months to reach sale weight, about 1.3 kg for a hen and 1.5 kg for a cock, so no bird goes from egg to sale in two months. Six production cycles a year in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference means six settings running at different stages at the same time: one batch in the incubator or under hens, one in the brooder for its first three weeks, one in the chick room, others in the grower compartments for the 3 to 6 month birds. That is also why the reference asks for at least five compartments: several ages are on the farm at once by design.

history.content: Six cycles a year means a bird goes from egg to sale in two months.

draws.answer: Not two months, it is about ten to twelve weeks for a hen and about twenty-one days for a cock, which is the minimum of the commercial model the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference gives, and it is the ratio the study uses for selling at its market value. The six production cycles a year is one cycle a year for two birds, which is the same reference's figure for keeping the flock, and it means a bird moves in and out of the unit twice a year rather than once. The two months you are describing are the incubation, which is the same reference's first year figure, 60 days, and the hatching is the second year figure, 80 eggs per hen. The selling at that time is a second year figure as well.

The figure is on the time, not on the size of the batch. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans a net result of 131 birds sold in the first year and 3,850,124 FCFA of first year working capital in 2020 prices, so a sale over six cycles is a net result of 131 times 3,850,124, not 6 cycles. The two months figure is the time from egg to sale, not how often birds are sold. The pattern you describe is the one the reference plans, not its size.

per_item.reference: Look under the leaves of your tomato plants every week to detect any tiny insects. Turn each leaf over and count the insects on a few plants before you decide on any spray. If the insects are numerous, prune the most infested leaves and destroy them. Remove weeds from the plot edges that can serve as a refuge for the pests. Use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies and a strong water jet to wash off aphids, while ladybirds and lacewings will naturally suppress them. For the approved product and dosage, contact ICAT.

history.content: The leaves on my tomatoes are yellowing and I hear a faint buzzing, what's the first thing I should do?

draws.answer: Those signs are typical of tomato sucking pests, so the first thing to do is shake the plant and look closely to identify the pest, because each needs a different treatment. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on several plants to decide if treatment is necessary. Remove the most heavily infested leaves and destroy them, and clear weeds around the plot edges. For whiteflies, set yellow sticky traps; for aphids, use a strong jet of water and encourage ladybirds and lacewings. If the infestation is severe, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

per_item.reference: From the Ministry and PASA catalogue of good practices. Year one, improving plants, the legumes that feed the soil with nitrogen: beans, groundnut, cowpea. Year two, a hungry plant that consumes a lot, maize, the soil now being rich in nitrogen. Year three, a root or tuber crop that goes for the nutrients left deeper, yam. Year four, an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, okra. Then back to year one with legumes. Before fixing it, take account of your soil's fertility and of last season's crop.

history.content: rotation 4 ans exemple

draws.answer:
Year 1: legumes, the improving plants that feed the soil with nitrogen, such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean.
Year 2: maize, the hungry plant that takes a lot, in the succession that follows.
Year 3: a root or tuber crop that goes down for the nutrients left deeper, such as yam.
Year 4: a fallow.

Year 1, legumes, year 2, maize: the catalogue's own example runs five years. Year 1 is grown here, as beans, groundnut or cowpea, and year 2 is maize. Year 3 is a root or tuber crop, yam. Year 4 is a fallow. Then the cycle starts again: year 1 is again legumes, year 2 is maize, year 3 is a root crop, year 4 is back to legumes. The rule behind it is the nutrient needs of each plant, with nitrogen being most of it.

per_item.reference: Transplant seedlings after about 21 days in the nursery, placing 2 to 3 plants per pocket spaced 20 by 20 centimetres. For lowland or irrigated fields, apply 200 kilograms per hectare of NPK 15-15-15 about a week after transplanting, then split 100 kilograms per hectare of urea, giving half at tillering and half at panicle initiation. Weed the field at 15 to 25 days after transplanting and again around 40 days. Protect the crop from birds from flowering until harvest. If you need variety matching or rate adjustments, see ICAT.

history.content: How should I transplant and fertilise my rice seedlings?

draws.answer: Transplant seedlings after about 21 days, placing 2 to 3 plants per pocket spaced 20 by 20 centimetres. Apply 200 kilograms per hectare of NPK 15-15-15 between 30 to 45 days after transplanting, then apply urea at 100 kilograms per hectare in two equal applications, one at 25 to 35 days and the other at 40 days. Weed the field at 15 to 25 days and again around 40 days. Protect the crop from birds from flowering until harvest. For variety matching and rate adjustments, see ICAT.

Transplant the seedlings after about 21 days in the nursery, putting two to three plants per pocket spaced 20 by 20 cm. Do not grow rice on the same plot for more than two consecutive years to reduce parasite pressure. Apply 200 kg per hectare of NPK 15-15-15 about a week after transplanting, then add urea at 50 kg per hectare split into two equal applications, first at tillering and second at panicle initiation, keeping the second application below the recommended rate. Weed the field at 15-25 days after transplanting and again around 40 days, then protect the crop from birds from flowering to harvest. For variety matching and rate adjustments, consult ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is not a pest problem; the maize is experiencing nitrogen depletion on a soil that has lost organic matter. First, look at the leaves: uniform pale yellow on the older lower leaves indicates nitrogen hunger. Second, avoid buying a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide based on a merchant's word, because mineral fertilizer alone often does not give a return on exhausted soil. Third, restore organic matter by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the proper dose for your plot. ICAT is the service to see.

history.content: My old maize field in Kara shows pale yellow older leavees while the new ones stay green, is it a pest?

draws.answer: The symptom points to nitrogen depletion in your maize. Begin by reading the leaves; the uniform pale yellow on the older lower leaves indicates a nitrogen hunger, not a pathogen. Next, restore organic matter by adding manure, compost, or by leaving residues in the soil rather than burning them. Do not purchase a broad-spectrum NPK or a systemic fungicide, as mineral fertilizer alone often does not pay back on depleted soils. Finally, include a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean in your rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. For a soil analysis and the correct dosage, see ICAT.

It is nitrogen hunger, not a pest or disease. Do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide because they will not fix the problem. First bring organic matter back by applying manure, compost, or by leaving residues in the soil rather than burning them. Then plant a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean and cut it at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally ask ICAT for a soil check and the correct dose for your plot. per_item.reference: Then the count against the floor may be fine and the compartment still wrong. Check the number first: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on 8 to 10 breeders per square metre, 12 to 15 growers and 50 chicks, so measure and divide before anything else. If you are inside the figure, look at why one end is unused. The reference wants the henhouse well aired and roomy, with a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m, three bricks at most, and tarpaulins kept to close against rain and wind, so a cold or wet end will empty. Check the feeders and drinkers are spread rather than grouped: for adults, one feeder of 150 cm by 12 by 16 for 25 birds, and four drinkers of 10 litres per hundred layers. And keep the compartments to their ages, since that is what the five compartment plan is for.

history.content: The birds are crowded at one end and the other end stays empty.

draws.answer: Then the difference is the ratio rather than the density: at least three times the commercial density, 8 to 10 birds per square metre. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives it, and it is written as one of the ratios to look at when you plan, not as a number to find out. For the housing itself, the 2017 ESFT compendium says to build an Improved Traditional Poultry House of banco or straw, with rooms of at least 4 m by 3.5 m, one for every hundred birds, and a fenced run around it.

That is the real problem before you think about the feed. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on a unit with one commercial unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, and its first year projection of 1,422 birds and 2,376 eggs sold in 2020 prices counts 60 hens and 6 cocks in it, so the empty end belongs there. The 2017 ESFT village compendium asks for at least 80 adult layers and 6 cocks for the commercial unit. Keep the end full by splitting the shared wall into compartments, offering smaller feeders to the chicks, keeping the water clean, and checking the droppings are in the shade and being washed.

per_item.reference: The symptom is nitrogen loss in maize, not a disease that requires roguing. Start by opening a shallow drainage channel so water runs off the plot instead of standing. When the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, and keep the fertilizer off the plant to avoid burn. Continue with the second weeding and earthing-up as scheduled. If you later see streaks or dead-hearts, you should see ICAT.

history.content: After a heavy shower my corn's lower leaves are pale, especially where water pooled. Should I remove the plants?

draws.answer: Yes, pull the severely affected corn plants out and destroy them to avoid spreading the disease. Then, for the next planting, plant a cereal on that same field and use the cereal as a fallow, since maize streak virus cannot be cured with any spray. Also, avoid sowing corn late because late sowing raises the risk of infection. For the following season, obtain a tolerant maize variety from ICAT. I cannot give you any other specific product or dose.

The pale lower leaves of your maize after heavy rain indicate nitrogen loss, not a disease. Do not remove the plants, because pulling them can spread the virus. Apply urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, using about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation and keep the fertilizer away from the plant to avoid burn. Also keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule as planned. If you later see streaks or dead-hearts, you need to see ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is bloat affecting your nanny goat. Immediately get the goat on its feet and keep it moving, holding its head raised to help belching. After that, drench a little vegetable or mineral oil into its mouth to break the froth and free the gas. This helps the rumen work again and lets the gas escape. The condition can lead to collapse very quickly. Call the veterinary service immediately for emergency assistance.

per_item.reference: Your cattle have gall sickness (anaplasmosis). Call the veterinary service the same day because only they can confirm the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet that the urine is yellow-brown without red, which points to gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in the shade, give it clean water within reach, and do not make it walk because it lacks red blood cells. Hand-pick all ticks you can see on the whole herd, not just the sick animal, to stop further spread. See the veterinary service the same day.

history.content: My cows are looking weak, they have yellow urine and seem to lag behind the herd.
Are the gums and eyelids pale or white?
Yes, their gums and eyelids are pale.

draws.answer: Your cattle have gall sickness caused by Anaplasma marginale. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can confirm the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet that the urine is yellow-brown without any red, which helps them identify the parasite. Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make it walk because it lacks red blood cells. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not only on the sick animal, to stop further spread. See the veterinary service the same day.

Your cattle have nagana, a trypanosomiasis spread by tsetse fly bites. Report the case to the veterinary service so they can confirm the diagnosis and give the correct trypanocide; do not guess a drug or dose. Reduce fly exposure by avoiding grazing in riverine bush during biting hours and consider fly control measures. Keep the animals well fed and watered to help them cope and recover. See the veterinary service for diagnosis and proper treatment.

per_item.reference: Waiting with a small bag of beans after the harvest can be profitable. First, make sure the beans are stored well dried to keep them in good condition. Then keep that bag instead of selling the whole harvest immediately. When the lean season arrives, roughly June through August, prices usually go up. Check the weekly market day for your village and follow SIM cereal price updates on the radio before you decide to sell. Compare the local price plus transport cost with the price you might achieve in Lomé or other large markets. If you can, join a cooperative or sell together to reach larger buyers and cut per-bag transport cost. For more assistance, approach a cooperative or ICAT, and also ANSAT for grain.

history.content: I have a small bag of beans left after harvest. Is it smart to wait before selling?

draws.answer: Waiting does not make beans better, and it also puts money into your pocket. The brochure says to do what you can about the store at the time of sale and to compare prices across markets, because a low price when you are ready is what lets you sell. Store well and keep a part of the crop past the season, if you can, so the price you are asked for is not the last figure. The study's own rows show 16,000 FCFA a bag in 2005 prices, and it notes that selling at the harvest glut is what lets farmers buy subsidised inputs at the market. If you want to learn the price this season, ANSAT is the service; ICAT also holds prices.

Selling after harvesting is not the wrong time. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference advises selling when the price is good, not on a specific date, and it warns against buying in the market during the lean season. After the harvest, move the beans to the storage area and keep them well dried. Then you can sell them again later at a better price. For the best current price, go to the nearest weekly market and ask a few sellers, and follow the SIM cereal prices on the radio to compare markets.
